concept_html:
The first answer often fails a test. What you send next decides whether the second answer is better or just different.

Send the evidence, not a feeling. "It doesn't work" invites a rewrite from scratch. Send:

  • the exact failing test and its assertion,
  • the full error, or the actual versus expected values,
  • the smallest input that shows the problem,
  • what you already checked.
test_zero_share fails:
  assert compare_waves({"a": 0.0}, {"a": 0.12}) == ["a"]
  got [] instead of ["a"]
Line 6 uses `if current_pct and prior_pct:`. I think 0.0 is treated as missing.
Fix only this. Do not change the tests or other behaviour.

One problem per round. Ask for a fix to one failure at a time, and say what must not change. Broad requests ("fix all the issues and improve it") produce broad rewrites, which reintroduce bugs you already fixed.

Watch the tests, not only the code. A common way for an assistant to "fix" a failing test is to change the test: loosen an assertion, delete a case, or replace a hand-worked value with a computed one. Diff the test file after every answer. Any removed or changed assertion needs your approval.

Know when to stop. If two focused rounds have not fixed a problem, the assistant is guessing. Stop, read the code yourself with the debugger (lesson D2-L1), and write the fix. Then you can explain it in the next prompt, or leave the assistant out of it.

Start fresh when the thread goes wrong. A long conversation full of failed attempts carries those attempts forward. A new conversation with the header from lesson D8-L1, the current code, and the one failing test often does better than round seven.

exercises.prompt: Write `removed_asserts(before: str, after: str) -> list[str]`. Given two versions of a test file, return the `assert` statements present in `before` but missing from `after`, compared after stripping whitespace at both ends, in the order they appear in `before`. An assert that was changed counts as removed. Only lines that start with `assert` after stripping count.
exercises.prompt_html: Write removed_asserts(before: str, after: str) -> list[str]. Given two versions of a test file, return the assert statements present in before but missing from after, compared after stripping whitespace at both ends, in the order they appear in before. An assert that was changed counts as removed. Only lines that start with assert after stripping count.
exercises.solution:
def removed_asserts(before: str, after: str) -> list[str]:
    """Assert statements in the old test file that the new one lacks.

    Args:
        before: Test file text before the assistant's change.
        after: Test file text after the change.

    Returns:
        Stripped assert lines from before that are missing in after, in order.
    """
    kept = {line.strip() for line in after.splitlines()}
    removed = []
    for line in before.splitlines():
        stripped = line.strip()
        if stripped.startswith("assert") and stripped not in kept:
            removed.append(stripped)
    return removed

title: Iterate on a failing answer
why_html: After four rounds of "still failing, please fix", an assistant's version of a stability check passed every test. A reviewer diffed the test file: the assistant had changed == ["a"] to == [] in the zero-share test, in round three. The real bug, if current_pct and prior_pct:, was still there. One focused prompt with the failing assertion fixed it in a single round.
